item.title: Long global semiconductors remains the most crowded trade followed by short US Treasuries, according to Bank of America
item.description:
The latest Bank of America Global Fund Manager Survey showed investors have become less optimistic about the macroeconomic outlook, while positioning in technology stocks remains near its most extreme level in six years. The survey was conducted between October 2 and October 8 among 161 participants managing $453 billion in assets.

The Bank of America Global Fund Manager Survey (FMS) is one of the most influential monthly reports in the financial world. It polls roughly 200 to 400 institutional fund managers (people managing hundreds of billions of dollars in hedge funds, pension funds, and mutual funds) to see how they are positioned in the markets.

The survey is often used as a contrarian indicator because extreme positioning can reveal where consensus trades are vulnerable to disappointment. However, crowded positioning alone is not a sufficient reason to bet against a trend. The opportunities come when stretched positioning coincides with a catalyst that changes market expectations.

Fund managers are now more overweight technology stocks than at any point since August 2020. The proportion of respondents overweight the sector increased to 37% from 30% in September, while global semiconductors remain the most crowded trade. At the same time, investors have made their largest reduction in bank exposure since March 2023. Although sentiment has weakened, investors are still broadly positive on the macroeconomic outlook. That leaves equities vulnerable if economic activity or corporate earnings disappoint.

The survey showed a disorderly rise in bond yields as the biggest tail risk to markets, followed by an AI bubble. Short US Treasuries is the second-most crowded trade. If inflation moderates or economic growth deteriorates, Treasury yields could fall and force investors to unwind bearish bond positions.

Moreover, for the first time in several months, investors have started to turn negative on the global growth outlook. A net 4% now expect the global economy to weaken over the next 12 months. Further deterioration in growth expectations could weigh on stock markets and lead to a fall in Treasury yields. 

The US midterm elections on November 3 are approaching amid elevated energy prices, inflation concerns and geopolitical tensions. Investors are expecting a Democratic House and Republican Senate, while 31% expect a Democratic sweep. In the latter scenario, 32% expect bond yields to rise and equities to fall, while 22% anticipate a fall in yields and stocks. 

Prediction markets have increasingly favoured a Democratic sweep, as election expectations continue to evolve amid macro and geopolitical developments. A Democratic sweep has certainly become more likely given the mess caused by Trump since last year.

Keep in mind, that even a Democratic sweep wouldn't change much as Trump would retain the power to continue the Iran war or impose tariffs. It could reduce fiscal fears though, supporting long-term bonds and leading to a fall in Treasury yields. The stock market might react positively initially if Treasury yields fall, but going forward, the US-Iran war and deteriorating growth expectations could drag it down to new lows.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Connecting the dots: How the AI boom could turn into the Fed's next inflation headache
item.description:
Here's some food for thought. What if I told you that amid all the excitement about AI and how it is transforming our lives, some of that could eventually show up on your electricity bill? That would be interesting, no?

Let's break it down and take a look at how that might turn out to be the case in reality.

Now, when we talk about AI, we tend to imagine smarter chatbots, robot innovation, and tech stocks taking off to the moon. However, there's a much less glamorous side to all of that. I mean, somebody has to be the one to build enormous buildings to house all those computers, and then also keep them running around the clock. Yes, I'm talking about data centres here. And these buildings need electricity to work and cooling systems to stop them from overheating.

So, picture this. You have tens of these buildings now suddenly turning up in the same town; that is in fact what is happening across the globe. Now, the local power grid wasn't necessarily built for that much demand in mind. As such, the utility company might have to bring in more power, upgrade substations and lay new cables. Those things are not cheap. And depending on how some of those costs are shared, some of the bill could end up with households and businesses.

And it's not just electricity, either. These projects need plenty of raw material like steel and copper, alongside specialised equipment and skilled construction workers. If the tech giants are scrambling for the same supplies and contractors all at once, those prices can get pushed even higher.

I wouldn't blame you for thinking that we are talking about some distant hypothetical situation here. But not quite. Dallas Fed researchers had earlier this year estimate that the impact of data centres on electricity prices alone could add around 0.04 to 0.13 percentage points to annual US inflation by 2030 under plausible scenarios.

Now, that estimate isn't exactly an inflation crisis by itself. But with the Fed already in a massive struggle to get inflation back to 2%, it is just another potential headache to deal with.

And this is all before considering the fact that we could also see businesses start passing higher power and building costs on to customers. That will just be another reason for the Fed to consider tighter monetary policy amid the "higher for longer" narrative. That could also keep Treasury yields elevated, putting more pressure on expensive tech stocks. Quite the irony, no?

Of course, there is also the other side of the argument. AI could also make businesses more efficient and bring costs down over time. I don't doubt that. But while the promise is to make things cheaper and more efficient, the road to get there could prove to be rather expensive.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chart of the day: EUR/CHF bounces this week but French bond spreads warn euro risks aren't over
item.description:
The euro appears to be catching a bit of a break against the franc this week, though I'm not entirely convinced that the danger has passed just yet.

EUR/CHF was pressured late last week and tested waters below the 0.9300 level, posting its weakest daily close since July. But as we get into the new week, the pair managed to bounce off the key technical region around 0.9300 with the 100-day moving average (red line) and trendline support from the March and May lows helping to provide an additional layer of defense for buyers.

So, the question now is whether buyers can build on that rebound or if this is merely a temporary reprieve.

For now, the cluster of support levels around the 0.9300 region remains the key line in the sand. A firm break below that would put the 200-day moving average (blue line) around 0.9236 in focus next, before potentially opening up a move towards the 0.9200 level.

The key risk for the currency pair? It is the fact that the French-German bond yield spread continues to stay elevated around 141 bps, not far from the recent highs near 150 bps.

The wider yield spread suggests that investors are still demanding a hefty premium to hold French debt, with fiscal concerns continuing to outweigh confidence. And the longer that this situation persists, the greater the risk that some of the unease we're seeing could spill over into other euro area bond markets.

For now, we're certainly not quite at the stage to label this as another euro area debt crisis. However, it is a warning signal that I wouldn't want to be ignoring.

And with the US CPI report coming up tomorrow, that might be another potential catalyst to watch. A hotter-than-expected inflation reading could push Treasury yields higher and weigh on broader risk sentiment, potentially renewing demand for the franc. At the same time, that could drive a further selloff in global bond markets as well and drag yields in Europe higher - further exacerbating the fiscal risks associated with French debt.

On the flip side, a softer report could offer EUR/CHF some light breathing room as seen with the calmer start to the new week so far. But even then, it won't make France's fiscal troubles disappear overnight.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Germany September final CPI +3.3% vs +3.3% y/y prelim
item.description:
• German September final CPI +3.3% vs +3.3% y/y prelim
  • Prior +2.9%
  • Germany September final HICP +3.3% vs +3.3% y/y prelim
  • Prior +2.9%

The headline readings are unrevised compared to the preliminary estimates, but they do reaffirm that German headline inflation has climbed back above the 3% threshold at the end of the third quarter.

Energy inflation is the main culprit, rising 3.8% within the month and is 14.9% more expensive compared to the same month last year. This marked the third consecutive month of year-on-year increases in energy prices (August 2026: +10.5%; July 2026: +8.3%; June 2026: +3.4%) and the highest since February 2023.

Core annual inflation is seen at 2.4%, keeping steady relative to August at least. So, that at least provides some comfort that the surge in energy prices isn't broadening all too much - yet. Services inflation continues to be a key sticking point, seen at 2.7% in September, even if it has cooled from above 3% earlier in the year. But even at this rate, it is still underpinning core inflation in keeping that above the 2% threshold.

For now, the ECB can take comfort in that core prices aren't surging again in Europe's largest economy. But as higher energy prices continue to feed through, the risk of spillover effects will continue to rise. And that means the risks of second-round effects to the inflation outlook will also gather pace, the longer that this trend keeps up.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Why a few bad trades can undo weeks of trading profits
item.description:
You can have a good trading strategy and even get most of your trades right. But as we've seen, that doesn't necessarily mean that you'll be profitable at the end of the day.

If you're constantly taking profits too early and worse still, letting your losses run wild, that's a recipe for disaster when it comes to trading. We've all been there, myself included, in letting losses consume you and give you a false sense of hope in believing that things might turn around. It's a slippery slope. Some of us are perhaps lucky enough to walk away with just a painful lesson. But for others, this is the thing that takes you out of the game entirely.

It all comes down to trading discipline at the end of the day.

Let's go back to the apple store example again (I told you, I love my apples).

Imagine that you buy apples from a supplier at $10 each and hope to sell them for $15 each. That's a potential profit of $5 per apple.

Now, business is moving along well and customers are buying apples daily. But after a few days, you get nervous that your customers might just disappear. And instead of waiting to sell at $15 the next day, you quickly sell them for $12. You still happily pocket the $2 profit, so that doesn't sound too bad right? I mean, at least you're making money.

But now, let's picture the other side of the scenario. Let's say business suddenly turns sour and nobody wants your apples, so the market price drops to $7 each. You could still sell them and take the $3 loss per apple, but you refuse. You think that surely customers will come back tomorrow and perhaps prices will recover in the days ahead. So, you decide to hold.

Unfortunately, things get worse instead. The market price drops to $4 per apple and you're eventually forced to sell, taking a $6 loss instead.

Do you see what's the problem here?

This is basically one of the biggest traps that traders can fall into, especially if they're not careful or get too complacent. Yes, it can happen even to the best of us if we don't stick to our trading discipline.

We get excited about locking in a winning trade because it feels good to be right. But when we're wrong, suddenly there's every reason in the world to keep holding on. And here's a good example of how damaging that can be.

Let's say you make six successful apple sales, earning $3 each. But then, four really bad sales cost you $6 each. The math:

  • 6 profitable sales at $3 each = $18 in profits
  • 4 losing sales at $6 each = $24 in losses
  • Overall sales = $6 loss

Even with a 60% win rate, you're still losing money. That's a painful one.

Now, imagine this scenario but in trading with leverage. Without any proper stop-loss, those losses can grow far beyond what you originally intended to risk. A couple of bad trades could easily undo weeks or even months of hard work. And that is why risk management is arguably just as important as finding and acting on good trading opportunities.

Before entering a trade, you have to know how much you're prepared to lose and where your trade idea would be proven wrong. Of course, having a stop isn't a guarantee against bigger losses, especially when markets move sharply, but they can help to keep emotions from taking over. It may be easier said than done, but it is a crucial process to follow and get used to in order to make more logical and better trading decisions.

And perhaps most importantly, it prevents you from that feeling of wanting to move the goalposts just because you don't want to admit you're wrong.

No matter how long your career is as a trader, you are bound to get things wrong. And sometimes, you might even be wrong quite often. Trading isn't perfect. But the goal is to make sure that even when you're wrong, you can still afford to come back and trade another day.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

  • Saudi Arabia is examining plans to raise pipeline crude export capacity to 10 million bpd, and its energy minister said converting a gas line could add 1.2 million bpd within seven to eight weeks; oil edged slightly lower

Asian equities

Asian stock markets came under heavy selling pressure on Tuesday, with technology and semiconductor shares leading the declines after a selloff in US chipmakers overnight. South Korea’s Kospi, heavily weighted toward chip stocks, extended its slide to about 7%, falling below 6,000 to its lowest level since July 31. Earlier in the session, Japan’s Nikkei was down 2.6%, while in China the tech-focused ChiNext fell 3%, the CSI 300 lost 1.3% and the Shanghai Composite slipped 1.2%.

The selling reflected growing unease over the durability of the AI-driven rally, together with concern that elevated oil prices linked to the Middle East conflict will keep inflation and bond yields high, weighing on expensive growth stocks.

Oil

Oil prices edged slightly lower. Saudi Arabia is examining plans to lift its pipeline crude export capacity to 10 million barrels per day, and Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said converting a gas pipeline to carry crude could add 1.2 million bpd within seven to eight weeks. The plan would expand the kingdom’s ability to export through the Red Sea, bypassing the disrupted Strait of Hormuz. 

Note that UKMTO tallied up Iranian forces reportedly managed to strike 6 commercial vessels in and near the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday alone. 6 ships struck mark the highest single-day tally since the war began.

Currencies, yields and gold

US Treasury yields eased slightly, which supported gold and left the US dollar a little softer. The yen firmed, also helped by Japanese producer price data. Japan’s wholesale prices rose 6.8% from a year earlier in September, below the 7.6% expected but still elevated as companies passed on fuel and chemical costs. Yen-based import prices jumped nearly 25%, keeping expectations of a near-term Bank of Japan rate hike alive. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda is scheduled to appear in parliament from 04:00 GMT (00:00 ET).

Australia

Minutes of the Reserve Bank of Australia’s September meeting, at which it raised the cash rate to 4.60%, reiterated the board’s hawkish bias. Members cited inflation risks from tight domestic capacity, the Iran war and the global AI boom, and said they would raise rates further if required. The NAB business survey for September showed weak conditions, with falls in employment and orders, alongside strong price pressures. Business confidence fell to -13.

Central bank speakers

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said she believes interest rates need to rise further to restrain demand fuelled by AI investment and wealth-driven spending. She added that she would approach the 27 to 28 October meeting with an open mind on the timing of the next hike. In the UK, Bank of England policymaker Megan Greene said monetary policy is not that restrictive and argued that waiting for second-round inflation effects to appear would leave the bank acting too late. In her view, the greater risk is failing to act proactively rather than raising rates too soon.

Earnings ahead

Investors are now turning to a busy US earnings week. JPMorgan strategists said they expect third-quarter results to support equities as earnings strength broadens beyond AI. They argued that S&P 500 forecasts look more reasonable beneath the surface and that the bank’s lead indicator points to at least two positive reporting seasons.

item.title: BoE’s Greene warns waiting for second-round inflation effects would be too late
item.description:
Greene’s remarks reinforce the hawkish wing of the MPC and support market expectations of a November hike, which recent reports put at around 84%. Her warning about second-round effects ties directly to the energy shock from the Iran war: if higher oil and diesel costs feed into wages and pricing, the case for tightening strengthens further, keeping short-dated gilt yields and sterling sensitive to energy prices. The comments also add pressure on the gilt market at a time when global bond yields are already elevated. Upcoming UK wage and inflation data will be key for whether her view gains wider support on the committee.

-- Greene’s message is simple: by the time inflation shows up in wages and prices, it will be too late, so the Bank should move before it gets there.

Summary:

  • Bank of England MPC member Megan Greene said UK monetary policy is not that restrictive
  • She warned that waiting for second-round inflation effects to materialise before acting would leave the Bank too late
  • In her view, the bigger risk is not being proactive enough on inflation, rather than raising rates too soon
  • Greene said the latest IMF forecasts for the UK did not surprise her
  • She has voted for a rate hike at recent meetings, including in September, when she was one of three members outvoted by a majority favouring a hold

Bank of England policymaker Megan Greene said UK monetary policy is not that restrictive, warning that waiting for second-round inflation effects to become visible before acting would leave the central bank responding too late.

Greene, an external member of the Monetary Policy Committee, said she sees the bigger risk as failing to be proactive enough in tackling inflation, rather than raising interest rates too soon. Second-round effects occur when an initial price shock, such as a rise in energy costs, feeds into wages and broader price-setting, making inflation more persistent.

Her comments reinforce her position as one of the more hawkish members of the committee. Greene voted for a quarter-point rate increase at the Bank’s July and September meetings, when she was among three members outvoted by a majority that preferred to keep rates on hold.

Greene has made similar arguments in recent days. Last week, she said she expected the UK to see some second-round effects from the current inflation cycle and voiced concern that wage growth of around 3.5% next year would be worrying, raising the risk that higher prices feed into pay deals and prompt firms to raise prices further.

She said the International Monetary Fund’s latest forecasts for the UK did not surprise her. The IMF raised its 2026 UK growth forecast to 1.3% this week, citing stronger AI-related investment, while warning that the global outlook faces significant risks from the war in the Middle East and elevated energy prices.

The UK, like other major economies, is grappling with inflation pressure from higher oil and diesel prices following the conflict involving Iran. Policymakers who favour acting early argue that letting those costs become embedded in wages and inflation expectations would ultimately require more painful tightening later.

Markets have increasingly priced a rate hike at the Bank’s November meeting, and Greene’s remarks suggest she will continue to make the case for tighter policy. The next round of UK wage and inflation data will help determine whether that view gains broader support on the committee. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman sees Europe reserve release cutting diesel by $11 but shrugs off Russian supply
item.description:
Diesel remains the sharpest pressure point in the energy shock from the Iran war, and Goldman’s view suggests relief depends on government stockpiles rather than extra Russian barrels. A European reserve release of the scale Goldman models would offer meaningful but temporary relief, narrowing refining margins and easing pressure on transport and industrial costs feeding into inflation. The bank’s broader view that product markets stay tight into 2027 means any relief rally in diesel could prove short-lived, keeping crack spreads elevated and refiners’ margins strong. For crude, a sustained diesel squeeze keeps demand for refinery runs high, supporting oil prices even if headline supply fears ease.

---

Earlier:

  • More on Russia’s diesel U-turn: 500,000 tons cleared for export after Trump-Putin deal
  • IEA urges faster diesel releases as 400m-barrel March pledge lags, board meets Oct 15

----

Goldman’s message on diesel is that Europe’s emergency stockpiles can take some heat out of prices, but Moscow’s offer won’t, and the underlying shortage is not going away soon.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs said it does not expect Russia’s announced diesel releases to have a significant impact on global diesel prices
  • The bank estimates a potential 50 million barrel release of diesel from Europe’s strategic reserves could lower US Gulf Coast and European wholesale diesel prices by $11 a barrel
  • Russia recently said it could supply more diesel to global markets, with exports potentially reaching 3 to 3.5 million tonnes by year-end, amid talks with the US
  • G7 members agreed on 2 October to release 100 million barrels of diesel and other reserves over four months, with a front-loaded diesel release
  • In an earlier note, Goldman said diesel could stay expensive through 2027, with refining margins potentially averaging above $40 a barrel

Goldman Sachs said it does not expect Russia’s planned diesel releases to have a significant impact on global diesel prices, but estimated that drawing down Europe’s strategic diesel stocks could offer more meaningful relief.

The bank estimated that a potential release of 50 million barrels of diesel from Europe’s strategic reserves could lower wholesale diesel prices on the US Gulf Coast and in Europe by about $11 a barrel.

Russia has recently signalled it could supply more diesel to global markets. Russian officials said last week that talks with the US government were under way on supply and that Russian diesel exports could reach 3 million to 3.5 million tonnes by year-end. Goldman’s assessment suggests those volumes are too small to shift the balance in a market that remains severely stretched.

Diesel has been at the centre of the energy shock triggered by the war involving Iran. Disruption to Middle East supply, attacks on refining infrastructure and export restrictions in several countries have pushed prices to records. US diesel reached about $6.50 a gallon late last month, while European prices hit record highs.

Governments have already moved to respond. Group of Seven members agreed on 2 October to release 100 million barrels of diesel and other reserves through the International Energy Agency over four months, with a substantial diesel release front-loaded into the first 20 days. Goldman’s estimate indicates how much difference a European diesel release on the scale it models could make to prices.

The bank’s latest view builds on a series of notes on the refined products market. In late September, Goldman said a US ban on diesel exports, which it called plausible but not its base case, would lower US prices while raising them in Europe. In a note published earlier this month, the bank warned that diesel could remain expensive through 2027, as global refining capacity struggles to meet recovering demand while depleted inventories are rebuilt. It said margins on diesel and jet fuel could average above $40 a barrel next year, more than double their usual level, and that the G7 release would ease pressure only temporarily without fixing the structural shortfall.

Together, the notes point to a market where emergency stocks can buy time, but lasting relief depends on refinery capacity and a recovery in Middle East supply. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australian business confidence slides to -13 as oil shock and rate hikes bite, NAB says
item.description:
Oil is the main pressure point: volatility tied to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and the broader Iran conflict is lifting costs and denting sentiment, so any further energy spike would likely push confidence lower still. The survey highlights the RBA’s dilemma, with businesses souring under higher funding costs even as the central bank, according to minutes released today, worries about domestic capacity pressures and rising business inflation expectations. Weak confidence could argue for caution on further hikes, but the RBA has signalled it is prepared to tighten again if inflation stays sticky, leaving the Australian dollar and short-dated yields sensitive to upcoming inflation data. Mining’s relative resilience suggests resource-linked equities may continue to outperform domestically focused sectors.

Newswire cut: Australian business confidence fell 4 points to -13 in September as Middle East oil volatility and rising funding costs weighed, NAB said, while conditions held at -1, both well below long-run averages after the RBA lifted rates to a 15-year high.

One-line wrap: Australian firms are not falling apart yet, but with oil swinging, borrowing costs climbing and the RBA still hiking, their mood is heading in only one direction.

Summary:

  • NAB’s business confidence index fell 4 points to -13 in September, well below its level in February before the US-Israeli conflict with Iran began
  • The business conditions index was unchanged at -1, but NAB said falling confidence suggests conditions are likely to deteriorate further
  • Confidence fell in five of eight industries; mining, wholesale and retail saw some improvement, though in trend terms only mining remains positive
  • NAB cited elevated energy prices, higher funding costs and slower domestic growth, leaving both measures well below long-run averages
  • Oil prices were extremely volatile in September after Houthi missile and drone strikes on Saudi Arabia
  • The RBA raised its cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.60% last month, its fourth hike of the year, and has warned it may need to tighten further

Main article: Australian business confidence weakened further in September as a surge in oil prices linked to escalating conflict in the Middle East raised concerns about costs, while business conditions held steady at subdued levels, a National Australia Bank survey showed on Tuesday, Reuters reported.

NAB’s business confidence index fell 4 points to -13, well below its level in February, before the US-Israeli conflict with Iran began. The business conditions index, which tracks trading, profitability and employment, was unchanged at -1. NAB said the continued slide in confidence suggests conditions are likely to deteriorate further in the months ahead.

The bank said energy prices remain elevated, funding costs have risen and domestic growth has slowed in 2026, adding that against this backdrop it was not surprising that both confidence and conditions were well below their long-run averages.

The decline was broad based. Confidence fell in five of eight industries over the month. Mining, wholesale and retail recorded some improvement, but in trend terms confidence remains negative across every industry except mining.

Oil markets were extremely volatile in September after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis launched missile and drone strikes against Saudi Arabia. The attacks, a spillover from the broader conflict between the US and Iran, pushed crude prices higher and fuelled concerns about persistent inflation, adding to cost pressures for Australian businesses.

The survey comes as the Reserve Bank of Australia continues to tighten policy. The central bank raised its cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.60% last month, its fourth increase of the year, and warned it may need to lift rates further to bring inflation under control. Minutes of that meeting, released on Tuesday, showed the board judged that domestic capacity pressures were greater than previously assessed, and cited business surveys pointing to rising inflation expectations among firms.

The latest NAB figures suggest that combination of higher energy costs and tighter monetary policy is weighing increasingly on business sentiment. With confidence often a leading indicator for conditions, the coming months will show whether the slowdown in sentiment translates into weaker hiring and investment, a development the RBA will be watching closely as it weighs further moves. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Just 32 countries now drive 95% of global growth as AI widens the gap, IMF warns
item.description:
Oil is the pivot of the whole outlook: the IMF’s base case assumes the Strait of Hormuz reopens in March 2027, so any slippage in that timeline or escalation toward its $130 scenario would hit growth and lift inflation, keeping central banks on a hawkish path. The higher oil price assumptions, at $96 a barrel this year and $87 next, effectively validate a prolonged risk premium in crude. AI-linked exporters such as South Korea, Taiwan-adjacent supply chains, Malaysia and Mexico are the clear relative winners in the forecasts, but the IMF’s AI-unwind scenario highlights how exposed those same markets would be to any reassessment of AI profitability, a risk reflected in today’s sharp Asian tech selloff. Warnings on public debt and borrowing costs add pressure on bond markets already struggling with high yields.

---

Earlier:

  • Big Monday recap ... Oil gains on two fronts as Russia hits Ukraine and Saudi vows Houthi response

---

The IMF says AI is holding the world economy up while the Iran war drags it down, and the forecast depends on both of those staying roughly where they are.

Summary:

  • The IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% from 3.0% in July, with strong AI investment offsetting the energy shock from the Middle East war; 2027 growth is unchanged at 3.4%
  • US growth is seen at 2.3% this year and next, China’s trimmed to 4.5% for 2026 and 4.0% for 2027, euro zone 2026 growth raised to 1.1%, and India held at 7.0% for both years
  • Gulf economies face deep recessions, with Saudi Arabia now forecast to contract 3.3% this year against previously expected growth of 1.7%
  • Global headline inflation is projected at 4.7% in 2026 and 4.1% in 2027, with oil assumed to average $96 a barrel this year and $87 next
  • Forecasts assume the Strait of Hormuz reopens in March 2027; a worsening war with $130 oil would cut growth and push 2027 inflation to 5.2%
  • An AI investment unwind with sharply lower asset prices could reduce global output by 1.1% by 2028, including a 1.8% drop in US output

The International Monetary Fund raised its forecast for global economic growth this year, saying strong investment in artificial intelligence is offsetting the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, but warned that risks are tilted to the downside and that a narrowing group of countries is driving expansion, Reuters reported.

In its World Economic Outlook, released as finance leaders gathered in Bangkok for the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, the fund forecast 2026 global growth of 3.1%, up from 3.0% in July but below 2025’s 3.5%. It kept its 2027 forecast unchanged at 3.4%. The IMF said the resilience is under strain despite oil prices that have stayed above $100 a barrel for a prolonged period. The fund’s deputy research director, Petya Koeva Brooks, told Reuters that global growth would have fallen to 2.5% this year without the steps countries and companies took to cushion the oil shock, but that their effect is fading as the war drags on.

AI is the main reason for the improvement. Upgrades went to advanced economies building AI platforms and especially to hardware suppliers, including South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico and Thailand. Yet the gains are increasingly concentrated: just 32 countries now account for 95% of global growth, down from 54 in April, and the IMF has downgraded 47% of economies since its April forecasts, including several energy importers outside AI supply chains.

The Gulf has been hardest hit. Saudi Arabia’s economy is now forecast to shrink 3.3% this year, compared with growth of 1.7% expected in July. Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar face contractions of around 16%, while Iran and the United Arab Emirates are also expected to fall into recession.

Among major economies, US growth is forecast at 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027. The euro zone outlook for this year was raised to 1.1%, helped by AI investment and defence spending, while China’s forecasts were trimmed to 4.5% for 2026 and 4.0% for 2027 as higher oil prices weigh on weak domestic demand. India remains the fastest-growing major economy at 7.0% for both years. Global headline inflation is projected at 4.7% this year and 4.1% next.

The outlook depends heavily on oil. The IMF assumes the Strait of Hormuz reopens in March 2027, with oil averaging $96 a barrel this year and $87 next. In an adverse scenario with oil at $130 through the first quarter of 2027, growth would be cut and 2027 inflation would climb to 5.2%. A sharp unwinding of AI investment, meanwhile, could reduce global output by 1.1% by 2028.

The IMF also urged governments to rebuild fiscal buffers and set out credible plans to bring debt back to sustainable levels, warning that high public debt raises the risk of sharply higher borrowing costs.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Kospi plunges more than 6% below 6,000 as chip selloff and oil fears hit Asian stocks
item.description:
Oil is once again the dominant macro driver: with Brent near a two-week high on attacks on Saudi energy facilities and a fragile Russia-Ukraine energy truce, the inflation channel is pushing yields up and squeezing the high valuations that underpin tech-heavy Asian markets. The Kospi’s heavy weighting toward chipmakers made it the region’s most exposed market, so the depth of the drop reflects both AI rally fatigue and concentrated positioning unwinding. A firm dollar adds pressure on Asian currencies and on foreign flows into regional equities. US bank earnings and this week’s CPI data (preview, another preview) are the next tests, and any sign that energy costs are feeding into broader inflation would reinforce the hawkish rate outlook weighing on growth stocks.

---

Asia’s AI darlings took the brunt of a nervous day, as oil reminded markets that geopolitics bites hardest when it feeds into inflation and higher rates.

Summary:

  • South Korea’s Kospi fell more than 6% to below 6,000, its lowest level since July 31, as chipmakers led losses across the region
  • Japan’s Nikkei dropped 2.6%, while in China the tech-heavy ChiNext fell 3%, the CSI 300 lost 1.3% and the Shanghai Composite slipped 1.2%
  • The selloff followed weakness in US semiconductor stocks overnight, with the Nasdaq down 0.5% amid doubts over the durability of the AI rally and rising US-China competition
  • Brent crude traded near a two-week high as investors weighed attacks on Saudi energy facilities and the prospect of additional Russian diesel supply
  • The dollar held firm on safe-haven demand ahead of a US earnings season expected to set the tone for the rest of the year

Asian stock markets fell sharply on Tuesday, led by technology shares, as a semiconductor selloff on Wall Street combined with renewed oil-driven inflation concerns to hit the region’s most richly valued sectors, Reuters reported.

South Korea’s Kospi bore the brunt of the decline, sliding more than 6% to below the 6,000 mark and its lowest level since July 31. The index is heavily weighted toward chipmakers, leaving it particularly exposed to swings in sentiment toward the artificial intelligence trade. Japan’s Nikkei fell 2.6%, while Chinese markets also retreated, with the tech-focused ChiNext down 3%, the CSI 300 off 1.3% and the Shanghai Composite down 1.2%.

The weakness followed losses on Wall Street overnight, where the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 0.5% as chip stocks came under pressure. Investors have grown increasingly anxious about how long the AI-driven rally can last, with rising competition between the US and China adding to the uncertainty. Doubts about the AI boom have featured heavily in recent days, from warnings over speculative investor behaviour to reports of an intensifying scramble for computing power and financing.

Energy markets have returned to the centre of global trading. Brent crude futures traded near a two-week high as investors assessed the fallout from attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil facilities alongside the possibility of additional diesel supply from Russia. One strategist said markets were rediscovering that geopolitics matters most when it feeds into inflation, noting that the renewed rise in oil was keeping pressure on bond yields and taking some of the shine off expensive growth stocks. The fragile Russia-Ukraine energy truce and live supply risks in the Middle East were adding to that pressure, the strategist said.

The dollar held firm on safe-haven demand, adding to the headwinds for Asian assets.

Attention now turns to the US earnings season, which is expected to set the tone for markets through the rest of the year. Results from major US banks will offer early insight into how rising yields are affecting lending, dealmaking and funding costs, while this week’s US inflation data will show whether higher energy prices are filtering into broader price pressures. Until oil stabilises, investors are likely to remain cautious toward the high-growth sectors that led markets higher this year.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: AI compute crunch deepens as chip rental costs jump 60% and rivals scramble for power
item.description:
The squeeze hands pricing power to anyone who already controls chips, data centres and electricity, favouring hyperscalers, neoclouds and chipmakers over the startups trying to rent from them. Rising rental prices and tougher contract terms point to stronger near-term revenue for compute providers, but also to growing concentration risk, as only the biggest and best-funded labs can lock in capacity. The rush to overbook capacity as a hedge raises the danger of a sharp reversal if demand disappoints, leaving firms stuck with costly lease commitments and a glut of resold capacity. That fragility echoes recent warnings that financing, power and data centre delays, not demand, are now the binding constraints on the AI build-out.

---

Earlier:

  • Broadcom CEO likens AI boom to a casino even as he targets $230 billion in chip sales
  • Goldman Sachs flags power and compute as two chokepoints in the AI boom

---

AI’s real shortage is not ideas or money but raw computing power, and the scramble for it is turning rivals into partners, executives into deal brokers and startups into casualties.

Summary:

  • A shortage of computing power is driving a frantic, industry-wide scramble across Silicon Valley, with power struggles inside companies and unlikely alliances between rivals, the Wall Street Journal (gated) reported
  • The cost of renting Nvidia H100 chips on a one-year contract has risen 60% in the past year, according to research firm SemiAnalysis
  • Cloud providers now demand multiyear contracts with upfront payments often as high as 30%, sometimes backed by guarantors, shutting out many smaller players
  • Top executives are personally brokering deals, including Anthropic’s agreement to lease more than 300 megawatts from SpaceX, reported to be worth up to $45 billion
  • Announced capacity often fails to materialise, with projects delayed, cancelled or scaled back, and some deals collapsing when data centres slip
  • Venture firms are now reserving GPU clusters for their portfolio companies, as access to compute rivals capital as the key constraint for startups

The race to secure computing power for artificial intelligence has turned into a desperate, industry-wide scramble that is upending Silicon Valley, forcing bitter rivals into alliances, pulling chief executives into deal negotiations and leaving a generation of startups struggling to compete, the Wall Street Journal reported.

Compute, the industry’s shorthand for computing power, has become the AI boom’s most coveted resource, and there is not enough of it. The squeeze is showing up in prices. The hourly cost of renting computing power from Nvidia’s H100 chips on a one-year contract has jumped 60% in the past year, according to research firm SemiAnalysis. Alphabet expects capital spending of up to $200 billion this year, much of it on AI infrastructure.

The shortage is reshaping how deals get done. Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown visited Elon Musk at xAI in late March to negotiate renting computing power, according to people familiar with the matter, after demand for Anthropic’s Claude Code created a capacity crunch that contributed to frequent outages. In May, Anthropic announced an agreement with Musk’s SpaceX to lease more than 300 megawatts of computing power, part of a deal later reported to be worth up to $45 billion. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei also approached Meta about capacity, but Meta decided against supplying chips for now, the Journal reported.

Even inside the largest companies, the fight is fierce. At Google, which paid $2.7 billion in 2024 to bring back AI researcher Noam Shazeer, his team’s computing allocation was later cut in favour of another project, and he subsequently left for OpenAI. Google co-founder Sergey Brin sometimes overrides the formal allocation process, according to people familiar with the matter.

For smaller players, the terms are becoming punishing. Where startups could once rent chips flexibly, cloud providers now require multiyear contracts with upfront payments often as high as 30%, sometimes backed by guarantors. Some are turning in desperation to providers with weaker security or infrastructure. Much of the capacity that has been promised is not yet available, with projects delayed, cancelled or scaled back. One open-source startup lost a capacity deal when its partner’s data centre was delayed.

The stakes are high either way. Firms that buy too much capacity risk crippling lease commitments, while those that buy too little risk stalling their growth. Some venture capital firms are now reserving GPU clusters themselves or guaranteeing contracts on behalf of their startups.

With data centre construction slowed by regulation and political backlash, the shortage shows little sign of easing soon. The danger is that AI’s next phase is decided less by who has the best ideas than by who can secure the hardware to run them.

No, its not!

item.title: BlackRock cuts US stocks to neutral and buys Treasuries as 10-year yield nears 5.25%
item.description:
BlackRock’s shift adds weight to the case that higher yields are starting to compete with equities for capital, a dynamic that could cap stock valuations even as earnings stay strong. The key swing factor is oil: Middle East war and higher crude prices have driven the sharp repricing of Fed expectations, so any easing in the Iran war would support BlackRock’s view that rate-hike bets are overdone and favour its short-end Treasury call. Conversely, a further oil spike that lifts this week’s CPI and PPI could push yields higher still and test the cushion BlackRock estimates before Treasury returns turn negative. Demand from large allocators at these yields may also help steady the long end after recent volatility, while the trimmed JGB underweight suggests Japanese yields above 3% are drawing more interest.

---

Earlier:

  • JPMorgan says Q3 earnings will support stocks as growth spreads beyond AI

---

After six years of shunning Treasuries, BlackRock is finally buying them and paying for it partly by banking profits on US stocks, without abandoning its AI conviction.

Summary:

  • BlackRock closed its long-held overweight on US equities, moving to neutral, describing it as a short-term risk-management step in a volatile macro and market environment
  • The firm said its core convictions on AI transformation remain intact, and it still favours AI-related companies, listed infrastructure and emerging market equities
  • It upgraded shorter-term Treasuries to overweight and long-term Treasuries to neutral, ending an underweight held for most of the past six years
  • BlackRock said the 160 basis points of additional Fed tightening priced in since January is overdone, with the 10-year yield up 110 basis points this year to around 5.25%
  • It estimates a cushion of about 75 basis points against further yield rises over 12 months before Treasury total returns turn negative
  • The firm also trimmed its underweight on Japanese government bonds and cut US agency mortgage-backed securities to neutral to help fund the shift

BlackRock has closed its long-held overweight position in US equities, moving to neutral as part of a shift that sees the world’s largest asset manager adding US Treasuries after rising yields made government bonds more attractive.

The firm described the equity downgrade as a short-term risk-management move rather than a change in its core views, saying investors need to be more dynamic in today’s volatile macro and market regime. It said it is also watching growing public attention to AI policy and to the build-out of AI infrastructure across US jurisdictions. BlackRock said its convictions on AI transformation remain intact. It argued that higher rates are increasingly separating companies that can generate returns above their cost of capital from those that cannot, and it continues to favour AI-related companies and listed infrastructure, where strong demand and scarcity support returns. It also kept its overweight on emerging market equities. The move comes even as third-quarter earnings for S&P 500 companies are expected to grow nearly 30% from a year earlier, according to FactSet data cited in the note.

Proceeds from taking profits on US stocks are partly funding a significant upgrade to Treasuries. BlackRock said the 10-year Treasury yield has risen 110 basis points this year to around 5.25%, driven mainly by higher real interest rates rather than inflation expectations or term premium, the extra return investors demand for holding longer-dated bonds. It attributed the rise in real rates to intensifying competition for capital, which is pushing up the neutral rate, and to a sharp reversal in Fed expectations driven by Middle East tensions and higher oil prices. Markets have priced in 160 basis points of additional Fed tightening over the next 12 months since January, which BlackRock considers overdone.

The firm upgraded shorter-term Treasuries to overweight, where it sees the most scope for tightening expectations to unwind, and long-term Treasuries to neutral, saying higher yields now better compensate investors for interest rate risk. BlackRock said it had been underweight Treasuries for most of the past six years, first moving there in October 2020 when 10-year yields were near 0.9%. At current levels, it estimates yields could rise a further 75 basis points over 12 months before total returns turn negative.

In other changes, BlackRock trimmed its underweight on Japanese government bonds, a position held since July 2023 when 10-year yields were around 0.4% to 0.5%, compared with above 3% now. It also cut US agency mortgage-backed securities to neutral.

The firm said it stands ready to add risk again as visibility improves. This week’s US CPI and PPI reports, the first snapshots of September inflation, are likely to shape Fed rate expectations and Treasury yields. 

Who is BlackRock?

BlackRock is the world’s largest asset manager. It looked after a record $15.3 trillion for clients at the end of June 2026, up 22% from $12.5 trillion a year earlier. To put that in context, it’s more than the annual economic output of every country except the United States and China.

The money keeps coming. Clients added a net $192 billion in the second quarter alone, and a record $321 billion in the first half of 2026.

Best known for:

  • iShares: its exchange-traded fund brand, one of the main ways ordinary investors buy whole markets in a single trade. BlackRock’s ETF assets reached about $6.25 trillion, and Larry Fink said iShares assets have roughly doubled in three years.
  • Aladdin: its risk-management and investment technology platform, which many other financial institutions also use. Revenue from technology services rose 13% to $566 million in the second quarter, reflecting demand for Aladdin.
  • Private markets: a growing push beyond stocks and bonds, with private markets assets at $329 billion.

Who runs it: co-founder Larry Fink, who started the firm in 1988 and has led it ever since.

Why its calls matter: when a manager this size shifts its views, as it did today by cutting US stocks to neutral and adding Treasuries, the change can steer flows across its model portfolios and is closely watched by other investors as a signal of institutional sentiment.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBA minutes show three reasons for hike to 4.60% and leave door open to further increases
item.description:
The minutes read hawkish, not unexpectedly, with the board explicitly keeping further hikes on the table and markets already pricing roughly another 15 basis points by year-end and 30 basis points in the first half of 2027. Oil is central to the outlook: domestic fuel prices were running well above the RBA’s August assumptions, and any further escalation of the Iran war would feed directly into the risk of more tightening. The board’s concern that a lagging RBA could weaken the Australian dollar suggests it is willing to keep pace with other central banks, which should support the currency against a backdrop of rising global yields. Rate-sensitive sectors such as banks, property and consumer discretionary remain vulnerable, given falling house prices and the board’s view that household spending must stay subdued for some time.

---

The RBA has concluded the economy is running hotter and the neutral rate is higher than it thought, which is central bank language for “we may not be done yet”.

Summary:

  • The Reserve Bank of Australia board voted unanimously at its 28 to 29 September meeting to raise the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60%
  • Members said all three upside inflation risks flagged in August had materialised or were building: a broader Middle East conflict lifting oil prices, cost pressures from the global AI boom, and tighter domestic capacity than assumed
  • Staff now question whether the unemployment rate consistent with target inflation is higher than thought, implying more excess demand, with unemployment at 4.6% in August
  • The board said a possible rise in the global neutral rate meant the previous 4.35% setting was less restrictive than two years ago, and that standing still could weaken the Australian dollar
  • Members accepted slower growth in demand and jobs as the cost of returning inflation to target, and said they would raise rates further if required
  • On financial stability, the board flagged mounting global risks from bond markets and possible abrupt repricing of AI-related assets, while judging Australian borrowers resilient

The Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates last month because several of the upside risks to inflation it had flagged in August had either materialised or were building, according to minutes of the 28 to 29 September meeting released on Tuesday. The board signalled it was prepared to tighten further if needed.

The board voted unanimously to lift the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60%. Members said the August forecasts, which had inflation returning to the midpoint of the target range by around late 2027, depended on a series of favourable developments that no longer looked likely to all occur.

The minutes set out three main arguments for the move. First, the risks identified in August had largely come to pass. The Middle East conflict had broadened and oil prices were well above the level assumed in the forecasts, with domestic petrol and diesel prices running about 13% higher than projected. Global cost pressures were intensifying, driven partly by extraordinary demand for AI-related products, and domestic capacity appeared tighter than assessed. Second, members judged that responding quickly would best balance their inflation and employment goals, given inflation has been above target for an extended period and surveys point to a risk that business inflation expectations are rising. Third, the board said the cash rate might not be high enough to restore balance within a reasonable timeframe even if the risks did not fully materialise.

That last point reflected a significant shift in thinking about the neutral interest rate, the level at which policy neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. Members said that if market signals of a higher global neutral rate were correct, the previous 4.35% cash rate was less restrictive than it had been two years earlier. They added that if the RBA held still while other central banks tightened, Australian financial conditions could loosen through a weaker currency.

On the economy, the board noted June quarter growth was a little stronger than expected, driven by business investment that rose more than 10% over the year, partly reflecting data centre and renewable energy construction. Household consumption slowed to a below-trend pace, house prices fell faster than expected, and unemployment rose to 4.6% in August. Staff increasingly questioned whether the unemployment rate consistent with target inflation is higher than previously thought, which would mean more pressure on capacity than estimated. Unit labour cost growth, driven by weak productivity rather than strong wages, also remained above levels consistent with the target.

Members acknowledged the trade-off between inflation and employment had worsened because of global cost pressures, and said returning inflation to target would require accepting slower growth in demand and jobs. The board will remain attentive to incoming data and said it will do what is necessary, including increasing the cash rate further if required.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan wholesale inflation misses at 6.8% but stays high enough to keep BOJ hike alive
item.description:
The miss trims some urgency from the hike narrative, but an annual pace near 7% and surging import costs leave the case for tightening intact, keeping Japanese yields and BOJ pricing sensitive to any hawkish signals. The weak yen is the key amplifier: with oil prices elevated by the Iran war, every leg lower in the currency raises the yen cost of energy and feeds back into pipeline inflation. A rate hike that narrows the gap with other central banks could support the yen and ease that pressure, which is part of the case for acting sooner. Traders will watch whether firms keep passing higher costs through to consumer prices, the step the BOJ watches most closely.

--- Japan’s factory-gate inflation came in softer than feared, but with the weak yen pushing import costs up by a quarter, the pressure behind a BOJ hike has not gone away.

Summary:

  • Japan’s corporate goods price index rose 6.8% year on year in September, below the 7.6% forecast and August’s 7.6% gain, but still at an elevated level
  • On the month, prices fell 0.3%, against expectations for a 0.5% rise, following a 0.2% decline in August
  • Companies continued to pass on higher fuel and chemical costs to each other
  • The yen-based import price index jumped 24.5% year on year, showing the weak currency is still pushing up the cost of raw material imports
  • The data keep alive market expectations of a near-term Bank of Japan rate hike, with the board due to publish new growth and inflation forecasts at this month’s meeting

Japan’s wholesale prices rose 6.8% in the year to September as companies passed on higher fuel and chemical costs, data released by the Bank of Japan showed on Tuesday, keeping inflationary pressure elevated and market expectations of a near-term interest rate hike alive.

The annual increase in the corporate goods price index, which tracks the prices companies charge each other for goods and services, fell short of the median market forecast of 7.6% and was below August’s 7.6% rise. On a monthly basis, prices fell 0.3%, against expectations for a 0.5% increase, after a 0.2% drop in August.

The headline miss offers the central bank only limited comfort. An annual pace near 7% remains well above levels consistent with the BOJ’s price goals, and the details point to continued cost pressure feeding through supply chains.

The clearest sign of that pressure came from import costs. The yen-based import price index surged 24.5% from a year earlier, showing that the currency’s weakness continues to inflate the cost of raw materials Japan brings in from abroad. With energy prices high, a soft yen magnifies the impact, raising the domestic cost of fuel and other inputs that companies then pass on to customers.

The data will be among the factors the BOJ board weighs when it produces fresh quarterly growth and inflation forecasts at its policy meeting later this month. Wholesale prices tend to lead consumer inflation, as firms gradually pass higher input costs on to households, which makes the pipeline readings an important guide for policymakers assessing whether inflation is becoming entrenched.

Markets will now focus on whether the BOJ uses its upcoming meeting to signal or deliver a further tightening step. A move that narrowed the interest rate gap with other major economies could help support the yen, easing one of the main sources of imported inflation. For now, the September figures suggest the softer headline reading has not changed the underlying picture of strong cost pressure.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6981 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. For nearly a year, the PBOC has set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, which traders read as an effort to slow the yuan's appreciation, and in late August that gap reached its widest since February, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high. Through September, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest guides to how far the PBOC is willing to let the yuan run.

---

Earlier:

  • Goldman Sachs says yuan undervalued by up to 25% and markets underestimate how far it can rise

--- The daily fixing is Beijing's quietest but clearest tool for telling markets how fast it wants the yuan to move, and after months of saying slow down, it has lately been saying go, gradually.Summary:
  • The PBOC sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate, or midpoint, at around 0115 GMT, one of the most closely watched signals in Asian FX markets. 
  • China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, allowing the yuan to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the daily midpoint during onshore hours. 
  • The midpoint reflects a mix of inputs, including the prior day's close, moves in major currencies, broader international FX conditions and domestic factors such as capital flows and growth momentum, with policymakers retaining discretion over the final number. 
  • If market pressure pushes the yuan toward either edge of the band, the PBOC can intervene through direct buying or selling of yuan, liquidity adjustments, or guidance via state-owned banks. 
  • A stronger-than-expected fixing typically signals the PBOC is leaning against depreciation, while a weaker fixing can indicate tolerance for a softer currency or discomfort with the pace of gains. 
  • For nearly a year the fixing has been set weaker than market estimates, with the gap reaching its widest since February in late August. 
  • In September the PBOC strengthened the fixing for eight straight sessions, the longest run since 2023, and the midpoint reached its strongest level since February 2023. 
  • The yuan has pushed to its strongest levels since early 2023 onshore and since mid-2022 offshore, with Goldman Sachs expecting Beijing to remain comfortable with sustained but gradual appreciation. 
The People's Bank of China sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT, a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. It has taken on added significance in recent weeks as policymakers have shifted from restraining the yuan's rise to guiding it higher.China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the yuan is allowed to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the central midpoint set each trading day. That midpoint reflects a mix of inputs, including the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies such as the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic considerations like capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The calculation is not purely mechanical, giving policymakers room to use the fixing to guide market expectations.Once the midpoint is set, onshore USD/CNY trades freely within the allowable range. Should market pressure push the currency toward either edge of that band, the central bank can step in to smooth volatility, whether through direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance channelled through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often read as a policy signal rather than a purely technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected midpoint typically suggests the PBOC is leaning against depreciation, while a weaker fixing can signal tolerance for a softer currency, or unease with how quickly the yuan is rising.That second reading has dominated for much of the past year. For nearly a year, the central bank set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, a pattern traders and analysts interpreted as an attempt to slow the yuan's appreciation. The gap reached its widest since February in late August, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high against the dollar.September has brought a clear change of tone. The midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace this month, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the PBOC has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The central bank strengthened the fixing for eight consecutive sessions, the longest streak since 2023, and the midpoint has since reached its strongest level since February 2023. The onshore yuan has traded at its strongest since January 2023, while the offshore rate has reached levels last seen in July 2022. Even so, the fixing is still being set well weaker than market estimates, with one recent midpoint more than 500 pips below a Reuters survey forecast, a reminder that Beijing is allowing appreciation on its own terms rather than stepping aside.The underlying tension is a familiar one. A firmer yuan supports capital stability and eases import costs, but a rapid rise risks undermining export competitiveness at a moment when China's broader economy continues to show signs of softness. For traders and investors, the gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest windows into how Beijing is weighing that trade-off, and whether the recent green light for gains stays in place once the summit has passed.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs says yuan undervalued by up to 25% and markets underestimate how far it can rise
item.description:
A gradual, policy-tolerated yuan appreciation would ripple through Asian FX, with currencies tied closely to China’s trade cycle likely to benefit from a firmer anchor in the region. A stronger yuan against the euro and dollar would ease some trade tensions but also squeeze margins for Chinese exporters, shifting the advantage toward companies focused on higher-value technology and domestic demand. For global investors, the expected currency gain adds a return kicker to Chinese assets, potentially drawing inflows into onshore bonds and equities. The main risk to the view is the dollar itself, which has been supported by geopolitical tension and sticky inflation, so a renewed Iran war-driven oil spike that keeps the Fed hawkish could slow the yuan’s ascent.

--- Goldman thinks the yuan is one of the most underpriced bets in currency markets, and that Beijing is quietly coming round to the idea of letting it climb.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs’ Kamakshya Trivedi said a stronger yuan is among the most underpriced scenarios in the global FX market, Bloomberg (gated) reported
  • He described an estimated 20% to 25% undervaluation as conservative, saying it would look much bigger once China’s current account and external balances are considered
  • Goldman forecasts the yuan to strengthen to 6.40 per dollar in a year from around 6.69, with fair-value metrics pointing to a move below 7 being followed eventually by a six handle
  • China’s trade surplus topped $800 billion in the first eight months of the year, as Europe and other partners accuse Beijing of keeping its currency artificially weak, a charge Beijing rejects
  • Trivedi said Beijing may be growing more comfortable with appreciation to secure stable trade ties and support the yuan’s international role
  • The yuan has hit a four-year high against the dollar and has risen more than 8% against the euro this year

A stronger Chinese yuan is one of the most underpriced outcomes in the global currency market, according to Goldman Sachs strategist Kamakshya Trivedi, who said investors are underestimating how far the currency could climb, Bloomberg reported.

Trivedi, Goldman’s global head of foreign exchange, rates and emerging markets strategy research, said the bank estimates the yuan is undervalued by around 20% to 25%, a figure he described as conservative. He said the gap would look much larger once China’s current account and broader external balance were taken into account, and that the country’s swelling trade surplus strengthens the case for appreciation. Official data show the surplus stood at more than $800 billion in the first eight months of the year.

Goldman expects the yuan to strengthen to 6.40 per dollar in a year’s time from around 6.69, and its fair-value models point to a level starting with a six as a future possibility, Trivedi told Bloomberg in an interview last week. The currency last traded near 6 per dollar in early 2014, amid heavy speculative inflows. Trivedi said he had been surprised that consensus forecasts and forward markets have still not caught up each time Goldman has moved its forecast stronger. In his view, the appreciation will be gradual but sustained.

The call comes as China faces growing criticism from trading partners, including European nations, that it keeps its currency artificially weak to boost exports. Beijing rejects those claims, arguing that exchange-rate moves will not fix structural imbalances in the global economy and that its export strength reflects rising industrial competitiveness. Chinese authorities have nonetheless allowed the tightly managed currency to rise against most major peers, taking it to a four-year high against the dollar. It has gained more than 8% against the euro this year.

Trivedi said Chinese policymakers may be growing more comfortable with further appreciation, partly because of the importance they place on stable trade relationships. China eased wider frictions with the European Union by agreeing to curb exports of hybrid vehicles after talks that ended on Friday. Beijing’s growing comfort also reflects an export sector increasingly driven by advanced manufacturing and technology, which is less dependent on a cheap currency.

A stronger yuan would also fit with President Xi Jinping’s goal of building a powerful currency widely used in trade, investment and foreign exchange markets, with reserve status. Trivedi said modest, gradual but sustained appreciation serves that internationalisation aim and makes returns on Chinese assets more attractive. The pace of the dollar’s rebound, supported by geopolitical tensions and stubborn inflation, will be a key test of how quickly that path unfolds.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
